1. Executive Summary & Review 1 Foundation Scope

This document serves as the exhaustive scientific companion and viva preparation guide for Group 15's 1st Academic Project Review on "AI-Based Structural Variant Prioritization from Long-Read Sequencing Using Explainable Machine Learning".

In this foundational milestone (~40% completion), the project scope is intentionally and rigorously focused on establishing the multi-dataset genomic infrastructure, proving the statistical significance of biological feature regimes, neutralizing fatal data leakage channels, and formulating a spatial chromosomal validation partition.

2. Slide-by-Slide Technical Reference & Deep Dive

Slide 01: Title Slide & Overview

Slide Purpose: Establish the project identity, project team (Group 15), core academic problem, and 1st review milestone boundaries.

  • Project Title: AI-Based Structural Variant Prioritization from Long-Read Sequencing Using Explainable Machine Learning.
  • Review 1 Goal: Establish the quantitative data foundation, validate statistical differences between pathogenic and benign SVs, eliminate data leakage risks, and define the machine learning prioritization framework.

Slide 02: Clinical Problem — The Structural Variant Interpretation Bottleneck

Clinical Context: Structural variants (SVs), defined as genomic alterations spanning ≥ 50 base pairs (including deletions, duplications, insertions, inversions, and translocations), account for the largest number of divergent nucleotides between individual human genomes (~10–20 Mb) and are the primary genetic drivers of rare developmental, neurological, and cardiovascular Mendelian diseases.

  • >20,000 SVs Per Genome: Long-read sequencing pipelines discover tens of thousands of candidate structural variants per patient.
  • The 40.0% VUS Barrier: In NCBI ClinVar, 40,741 out of 101,891 structural variants (40.0%) are cataloged as "Variants of Uncertain Significance" (VUS). Clinicians cannot determine whether these variants are pathogenic disease drivers or benign polymorphic background.
  • Unsustainable Manual Curation: Standard ACMG/ClinGen manual scoring requires extensive literature review and expert panel deliberation, taking days per patient case.

Slide 03: Motivation — Long-Read Sequencing & Explainable AI

Technological Convergence:

  • Why Long-Read Sequencing? Third-generation platforms (Pacific Biosciences HiFi circular consensus sequencing and Oxford Nanopore ultra-long reads) generate continuous reads exceeding 10 kb to >100 kb. These long reads effortlessly span repetitive transposable elements (LINEs, SINEs, Alu elements) and segmental duplications where short-read Illumina sequencing fails due to mapping ambiguity. Modern SV callers (Sniffles2, cuteSV, PBSV) resolve breakpoint boundaries at single-base or near-single-base resolution.
  • Why Explainable Machine Learning? A black-box classifier is unacceptable in clinical diagnostics. Our framework computes a continuous Prioritization Index (0.00 - 1.00) and utilizes TreeSHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) to output patient-specific waterfall plots detailing exactly how much population frequency, gene constraint, and deletion length contributed to the classification.

Slide 04: Literature Foundation & Background

Domain Key Reference Contributions & Inherent Limitations
Clinical Standards Riggs et al., Genetics in Medicine 2020 Establishes ACMG/ClinGen 5-tier point rubric for constitutional CNVs. Highly reliant on manual expert curation; struggles with non-coding SVs and complex events.
Population Baseline Collins et al., Nature 2020 gnomAD SV v2.1 benchmark (387,477 SVs across 10,847 diverse genomes). Proves that 90.12% of SVs in healthy individuals are rare (AF < 1%).
Computational Scorers AnnotSV, CADD-SV, StrVCTVRE AnnotSV compiles annotations; CADD-SV computes heuristic impact. Many past ML models suffer from severe post-diagnostic metadata leakage and lack patient-specific local explainability.

Slide 05: Research Gaps in Current Practice

  • Gap 1 (The 40% VUS Dilemma): Ambiguous clinical variants lack continuous statistical risk scoring for prioritization.
  • Gap 2 (Severe Metadata Leakage): Existing tools often include ClinVar review stars or submitter counts during training, achieving artificially high accuracy that collapses on real-world raw patient VCFs.
  • Gap 3 (Genomic Locus Leakage): Standard random 80/20 train/test splits allow variants overlapping the same gene or CNV hotspot (e.g. 22q11.2) to appear in both sets, masking model memorization.
  • Gap 4 (Diagnostic Opacity): Clinical adoption requires transparent, additive feature attributions rather than uninterpretable probability outputs.

  • Deletions & Copy Number Loss: 58.1% of all records (45,862 Deletions + 23,892 CN Loss). Highly enriched for pathogenicity due to haploinsufficiency.

  • Pathogenic Median Length: 51,100 bp (51.1 kb); Interquartile Range (IQR): 2.9 kb – 1.58 Mb.
  • Benign Median Length: 153,420 bp (153.4 kb); Interquartile Range (IQR): 56.2 kb – 401.2 kb.
  • Bimodal Pathogenic Profile:
    1. Focal coding disruptions (1 kb – 10 kb): Single-exon deletions causing frameshifts in dosage-sensitive genes.
    2. Megabase chromosomal syndromes (>1 Mb): Large multi-gene deletions causing severe developmental syndromes (e.g. DiGeorge 22q11.2, Williams-Beuren 7q11.23).
    3. Benign intermediate clustering (50 kb – 300 kb): Benign polymorphisms cluster in non-coding intergenic segments.

Slide 11: Population Allele Frequencies & Purifying Selection

Figure 4: Population allele frequency spectrum across 387,477 gnomAD SV sites showing extreme purifying selection.
  • 90.12% Rare (AF < 1%): 349,202 SV sites are observed at <1% frequency across 10,847 healthy genomes.
  • 39.39% Singletons (AF ≤ 0.0046%): 152,640 SVs appear exactly once in the entire dataset.
  • Purifying Selection: 91.8% of Loss-of-Function (LoF) SVs and 84.3% of promoter SVs are ultra-rare (AF < 0.1%). In contrast, intergenic SVs are frequently common (AF > 1%).
  • Key Biological Rule: High population allele frequency (AF ≥ 1%) is a nearly definitive negative predictor of clinical pathogenicity.

Slide 12: Statistical Hypothesis Testing — Formal Biological Proofs

Hypothesis 1: SV Length vs. Pathogenicity (Mann-Whitney U Test)

  • Null Hypothesis (H0): Pathogenic and benign SVs share identical genomic length distributions.
  • Test Statistic: U = 2.69 x 10^8
  • p-value: 3.04 x 10^-77 (Statistically Significant, p < 10^-5).
  • Conclusion: Reject H0. Genomic length is a statistically validated predictor of clinical outcome.

Hypothesis 2: SV Type vs. Pathogenicity (Pearson's Chi-Square Test)

  • Null Hypothesis (H0): Structural variant type is independent of clinical classification.
  • Contingency Breakdown: Deletions (23,781 Path vs 624 Benign); Duplications (5,479 Path vs 7,579 Benign).
  • Degrees of Freedom: dof = 11
  • Test Statistic: Chi-Square = 15,769.58
  • p-value: 0.0000 (p < 10^-300, Statistically Significant).
  • Conclusion: Reject H0. SV type is non-randomly associated with clinical severity.

Slide 13: Cross-Dataset Harmonization & Overlap Protocol

The Identification Mismatch:

  • Exact ID matching yields 0.0% overlap because ClinVar, dbVar, and gnomAD utilize independent, disjoint accession systems.
  • Strict breakpoint matching (≤ 100 bp) yields only 0.38% match due to legacy array coordinate uncertainty (± 50 - 500 bp).

Standardized Hierarchical Protocol:

  1. Coordinate Standardization: LiftOver all gnomAD GRCh37 coordinates to GRCh38.
  2. SV Type Concordance: Require exact type matching (DEL == DEL, DUP == DUP).
  3. Large CNVs (>5 kb): Require ≥ 70% reciprocal overlap [Overlap / min(len1, len2) ≥ 0.70].
  4. Focal SVs (500 bp – 5 kb): Require ≥ 50% reciprocal overlap.
  5. Unmatched Variants: Assigned AF = 0.0 (reflecting extreme population rarity).

Slide 15: Chromosomal Validation Strategy & Modeling Architecture

Spatial Independence Partitioning: Standard random splits cause genomic locus leakage because overlapping SVs in the same gene or recurrent microdeletion hotspot (e.g. 22q11.2) appear in both training and test sets. By partitioning strictly by chromosome, we guarantee 0.0% locus overlap:

  • Training Fold (Chromosomes 1–14): 25,158 unique SVs (~65% of data) — Representation learning & weight updates.
  • Validation Fold (Chromosomes 15–18): 8,546 unique SVs (~15% of data) — Hyperparameter tuning & probability calibration.
  • Holdout Test Fold (Chromosomes 19–22, X, Y): 8,854 unique SVs (~20% of data) — Unseen chromosome generalization benchmark.

Planned Model Suite (Review 2 Benchmarks):

  • Linear Baseline: L2-Regularized Logistic Regression (evaluates linear feature separability).
  • Tree Ensembles: Balanced Random Forest, LightGBM, and XGBoost configured with scale_pos_weight = 3.4.
  • Evaluation Metric: PR-AUC (Precision-Recall Area Under Curve) over ROC-AUC to prioritize true positive detection under 3.4:1 imbalance.
  • Interpretability: TreeSHAP exact Shapley attributions for all test predictions.

3. Mathematical & Statistical Formulas & Formal Derivations

1. Mann-Whitney U Test (Wilcoxon Rank-Sum)

The Mann-Whitney U test is a non-parametric test evaluating whether randomly selected values from population X (Pathogenic SV lengths) tend to be larger or smaller than values from population Y (Benign SV lengths). It does not assume a normal distribution, making it ideal for heavily skewed genomic lengths spanning 50 bp to >10 Mb.

Mathematical Formulation:
Let n1 be the number of pathogenic variants (n1 = 45,277) and n2 be the number of benign variants (n2 = 13,306). All N = n1 + n2 = 58,583 observations are ranked jointly in ascending order. The test statistics are:

• U1 = R1 - [n1 × (n1 + 1)] / 2
• U2 = R2 - [n2 × (n2 + 1)] / 2
• U = min(U1, U2) = 2.69 × 10^8

Under the null hypothesis, for large sample sizes, U asymptotically follows a normal distribution with:
• Mean (μ_U) = (n1 × n2) / 2
• Standard Deviation (σ_U) = √[ (n1 × n2 × (n1 + n2 + 1)) / 12 ]
• Z = (U - μ_U) / σ_U ⇒ p = 3.04 × 10^-77

2. Pearson's Chi-Square Contingency Test of Independence

The Chi-Square test tests whether structural variant type and clinical pathogenicity are independent nominal variables.

Mathematical Formulation:
For a contingency table with r rows (SV types, r = 12) and c columns (Clinical classes, c = 2):

• Χ^2 = ∑ [ (O_ij - E_ij)^2 / E_ij ]
where O_ij is the observed count and E_ij = (Row_Total_i × Col_Total_j) / Grand_Total is the expected count under independence.

• Degrees of Freedom (dof) = (r - 1) × (c - 1) = (12 - 1) × (2 - 1) = 11
• Χ^2 = 15,769.58, p = 0.0000 (p < 10^-300)

Odds Ratio for Deletions vs Duplications:
Odds Ratio (OR) = (Pathogenic_DEL × Benign_DUP) / (Benign_DEL × Pathogenic_DUP) = (23,781 × 7,579) / (624 × 5,479) ≈ 4.8×

3. Reciprocal Overlap Metric

Given two genomic intervals A = [start_A, end_A] and B = [start_B, end_B] on the same chromosome:

• Overlap(A, B) = max(0, min(end_A, end_B) - max(start_A, start_B))
• Reciprocal Overlap Fraction = Overlap(A, B) / min(length(A), length(B)) ≥ θ

Thresholds applied: θ = 0.70 for CNVs >5 kb; θ = 0.50 for focal SVs (500 bp – 5 kb).

4. 25 Comprehensive Viva / Examiner Questions & Model Answers

Q1: What is the formal definition of a structural variant, and why do long reads resolve them better than short reads?
A structural variant (SV) is any genomic alteration spanning ≥ 50 base pairs, including deletions, duplications, insertions, inversions, and translocations. Short-read Illumina sequencing generates 150 bp reads that cannot span repetitive elements (such as Alu, LINE-1, and segmental duplications), leading to ambiguous multi-mapping (mapQ = 0) and missing breakpoints. In contrast, long-read sequencing (PacBio HiFi / Oxford Nanopore) yields continuous reads of 10 kb to >100 kb that span entire repeat regions, enabling single-base breakpoint resolution.
Q2: Why is the 40% VUS proportion considered a major clinical bottleneck?
In NCBI ClinVar, 40,741 out of 101,891 structural variants (40.0%) are classified as Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS). When a patient receives a VUS in a clinical genetic report, clinicians cannot determine if the variant is causing the patient's disease or if it is a harmless polymorphism. This creates diagnostic uncertainty and delays treatment. Our project builds an explainable AI model to compute continuous risk scores and triage these 40,741 VUS into actionable tiers.
Q3: Why did you not include VUS variants in your binary training labels (Y = 0/1)?
Including VUS in binary training labels introduces severe label noise. If an ambiguous variant is arbitrarily assigned a label of 0 or 1, gradient updates in supervised models will be penalized on uncertain ground truth. Instead, we train exclusively on high-confidence Pathogenic (N = 45,277) vs Benign (N = 13,306) variants, and then use the trained model to rank and prioritize the 40,741 VUS during inference.
Q4: What is the class imbalance ratio in your training set, and how will you handle it?
The ratio is 3.40 : 1 (45,277 Pathogenic vs 13,306 Benign). In Phase 2, we handle this by configuring tree ensembles with scale_pos_weight = 3.4, using Balanced Random Forests, optimizing Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC) rather than ROC-AUC, and tuning probability decision thresholds.
Q5: Why did you split your data by chromosomes rather than using a random 80/20 train/test split?
In genomics, standard random splitting causes severe spatial data leakage. Multiple patients in ClinVar often share overlapping structural variants in the exact same gene or recurrent microdeletion hotspot (e.g. 22q11.2, 16p11.2). A random split would place identical genomic loci in both training and test sets, causing the model to achieve artificially high accuracy through locus memorization. By holding out entire chromosomes (Chr 19–22, X, Y), we guarantee 0.0% locus overlap and prove true generalization to unseen chromosomes.
Q6: What is data leakage, and what specific features did you drop from ClinVar?
Data leakage occurs when features contain information that would only be available after the clinical diagnosis is already made. We dropped: (1) ReviewStatus stars (reflects curation confidence), (2) PhenotypeList / Disease strings (explicitly encodes diagnosis), and (3) NumberSubmitters (proxy for clinical attention). Including these causes the model to learn curation metadata rather than biology.
Q7: Why did you transform raw gene symbol text into constraint scores?
Raw gene symbols represent high-cardinality categorical variables (>19,000 human genes). If one-hot encoded, tree models overfit by memorizing specific cancer/disease gene names (e.g., TP53, BRCA1). If a test variant appears in an uncurated gene, the model fails. Replacing gene names with continuous constraint scores (pLI and LOEUF from gnomAD) forces the model to learn the generalizable biological principle of dosage sensitivity.
Q8: What do pLI and LOEUF measure biologically?
pLI (Probability of Loss-of-Function Intolerance): Measures the likelihood that a gene cannot tolerate heterozygous loss-of-function variants. Genes with pLI ≥ 0.9 are haploinsufficient. LOEUF (Loss-of-function Observed/Expected Upper bound Fraction): A continuous metric where lower values indicate stronger purifying selection against loss-of-function variants (LOEUF < 0.35 indicates extreme constraint).
Q9: What was the result of your Mann-Whitney U test on genomic lengths?
The Mann-Whitney U test comparing pathogenic SV lengths (median 51.1 kb) vs benign SV lengths (median 153.4 kb) yielded U = 2.69 × 10^8 and p = 3.04 × 10^-77. Because p < 10^-5, we rejected the null hypothesis, formally proving that pathogenic and benign SVs occupy distinct genomic size regimes.
Q10: Why do pathogenic structural variants show a bimodal length distribution?
Pathogenic SVs fall into two distinct biological classes: (1) Focal coding disruptions (1 kb – 10 kb): precise deletions that disrupt critical single exons or cause frameshifts in dosage-sensitive genes; and (2) Megabase chromosomal deletions (>1 Mb): large multi-gene copy number losses that delete entire developmental chromosomal regions. Benign polymorphisms cluster in intermediate non-coding segments (50 kb – 300 kb).
Q11: What was the result of your Pearson's Chi-Square test on variant types?
The Chi-Square test yielded Χ^2 = 15,769.58 with dof = 11 and p = 0.0000 (p < 10^-300). This confirmed that structural variant type is non-randomly associated with clinical outcome. Deletions show 4.8x higher pathogenic odds compared to duplications of equal length due to haploinsufficiency.
Q12: Why did direct ID string matching between ClinVar and gnomAD fail with 0.0% overlap?
ClinVar uses internal numeric Allele/Variation IDs, dbVar uses accession strings (nsv/esv), and gnomAD generates coordinate-based synthetic strings (e.g. gnomAD-SV_v2.1_DEL_chr1_102). Because there is no universal primary key across databases, cross-repository integration requires coordinate-based reciprocal overlap matching.
Q13: Why did strict 100 bp breakpoint matching yield only a 0.38% match between databases?
Legacy ClinVar records were generated using chromosomal microarrays and short-read sequencing, which have breakpoint uncertainty windows of ± 50 to 500 bp. Strict base-pair matching fails; therefore, a hierarchical reciprocal overlap protocol (≥ 70% for large CNVs, ≥ 50% for focal SVs) is required.
Q14: What is purifying selection, and how does it manifest in gnomAD SV?
Purifying selection is the evolutionary pressure that eliminates deleterious alleles from the population gene pool. In gnomAD SV, 91.8% of Loss-of-Function SVs and 84.3% of promoter SVs are ultra-rare (AF < 0.1%). Highly functional SVs are suppressed by natural selection, making high population frequency (AF ≥ 1%) a strong negative predictor of pathogenicity.
Q15: Why is dbVar not used as a third independent feature source in your primary training set?
Our data audit revealed that dbVar clinical VCFs duplicate ClinVar submissions without adding new quantitative features (99.8% of experimental assay metadata columns are unpopulated). Therefore, ClinVar (ground truth labels) + gnomAD SV (population allele frequencies) forms our clean, non-redundant feature matrix.
Q16: What models will be benchmarked in Phase 2, and what is the baseline?
We will benchmark L2-Regularized Logistic Regression (as the linear baseline) against Balanced Random Forest, LightGBM, and XGBoost. This will evaluate whether complex non-linear feature interactions (such as size interacting with gene constraint) improve classification performance over linear models.
Q17: Why is PR-AUC preferred over ROC-AUC for this project?
ROC-AUC is known to be overly optimistic on imbalanced datasets because the False Positive Rate denominator (FP + TN) is dominated by the large negative class. Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC) evaluates Precision [TP / (TP + FP)] against Recall [TP / (TP + FN)], focusing directly on the clinical priority of detecting true pathogenic variants without excessive false alarms.
Q18: What is TreeSHAP, and why is it preferred over LIME or KernelSHAP?
TreeSHAP is an exact, polynomial-time algorithm [O(TLD^2) complexity] for computing Shapley values in tree ensembles. Unlike LIME (which uses local linear sampling approximations that can be unstable) or KernelSHAP (which requires exponential sampling), TreeSHAP guarantees the game-theoretic axioms of efficiency, symmetry, dummy player, and additivity, providing exact and consistent local feature attributions for every patient prediction.
Q19: How will the trained model prioritize the 40,741 VUS variants?
The calibrated model will assign each VUS a continuous risk probability from 0.00 to 1.00. We will categorize variants into 4 actionable triage tiers: Tier 1 (High Risk, score ≥ 0.80), Tier 2 (Moderate Risk, 0.50 - 0.79), Tier 3 (Low Risk, 0.20 - 0.49), and Tier 4 (Likely Benign, < 0.20), accompanied by TreeSHAP waterfall explanation plots.
Q20: What is LiftOver, and why was it necessary in data harmonization?
LiftOver is a bioinformatics tool that converts genomic coordinates between reference genome builds using pairwise alignment chain files. gnomAD SV v2.1 coordinates are aligned to GRCh37 (hg19), whereas modern clinical long-read sequencing uses GRCh38 (hg38). Lifting over coordinates to GRCh38 ensures correct spatial intersection without false positional discordance.
Q21: If a patient has a 1 Mb duplication overlapping non-coding regions with AF = 0.0, how will the model score it?
Even though the duplication is large and rare, because duplications have lower pathogenic odds than deletions and the variant does not overlap coding exons of constrained genes (pLI ≈ 0, LOEUF > 1.0), the model will assign it a lower risk score. TreeSHAP will show that while rarity pushed the score up, lack of gene constraint and duplication type pushed the score back down.
Q22: How will your tool integrate into a real hospital or genetics lab workflow?
We are developing a lightweight Python CLI and web interface. A bioinformatician inputs a patient's raw long-read VCF file (from Sniffles2 or cuteSV). The pipeline annotates each SV with gnomAD frequency and gene constraint, executes the trained XGBoost model, and outputs a ranked clinical HTML report highlighting Tier 1 variants with interactive TreeSHAP waterfall charts.
Q23: What are the primary milestones scheduled for Review 2?
For Review 2, our milestones are: (1) Complete classifier training and hyperparameter tuning on the chromosomal training fold; (2) Benchmark PR-AUC on the holdout test chromosomes (Chr 19–22, X, Y); (3) Generate global TreeSHAP beeswarm summaries; (4) Score and prioritize all 40,741 ClinVar VUS; and (5) Develop the patient VCF CLI tool prototype.
Q24: What is the main takeaway from your Review 1 milestone presentation?
We have established a rigorous, factually validated data and statistical foundation: ingested 101k ClinVar, 387k gnomAD, and 79k dbVar records; statistically proved size (p = 3.04 × 10^-77) and variant type (p < 10^-300) differences; neutralized 4 fatal data leakage channels; and structured a 0.0% locus overlap chromosomal partition ready for unbiased model benchmarking.
Q25: Why is Group 15 well-positioned to complete Phase 2 successfully?
Because all data harmonization, statistical proofs, leakage-free feature stores, and chromosomal splits are already completed, Phase 2 can proceed immediately to model optimization, TreeSHAP interpretability, and clinical tool development without any data pipeline bottlenecks.
